analysis.one_liner: Lets personal investment accounts grow tax-free until earnings are withdrawn.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted only two cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the tax code to create a new kind of personal investment trust whose earnings are exempt from federal income tax while the money stays in the account. The account must hold cash, cannot be invested in life insurance, and must be administered by a bank or an approved trustee. When earnings are paid out, they are taxed as ordinary income, though money can be rolled into another account tax-free. In effect, it is a tax-deferral vehicle for investment gains.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with spare cash to invest, since investment earnings would compound untaxed until withdrawal — a benefit that grows with the size of the account. Banks and trust companies would gain a new line of business, because the bill requires every account to be administered by a bank or an approved trustee.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors with cash to spare; banks

how_it_helps.text: Any qualifying 'tax deferred account' is exempt from federal income tax while it holds assets, so investment earnings and realized gains accumulate without being taxed year to year.
Earnings are taxed only when distributed, and as ordinary income; distributions rolled into another qualifying account within 60 days are not taxed.
The account balance is nonforfeitable, transfers to a divorced spouse are not taxable events, and trustees must report contributions and distributions to both the Treasury and the investor.
The bill places few limits on the accounts: it requires cash contributions and bans life insurance investment, but sets no cap on how much can be sheltered.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would collect less tax on investment earnings during the years money sits in these accounts, leaving other taxpayers to make up the difference. Because the accounts have no contribution limit, the largest tax benefits would go to the households with the most money to shelter.

drawbacks.text: Because there is no limit on contributions, the deferral benefit scales with wealth: a household able to park a large sum in the account shelters far more investment income than a typical saver, and the deferred revenue falls on other taxpayers.

The benefit is deferral, not exemption — earnings are taxed as ordinary income when paid out — so for a small saver the gain over simply paying tax each year is modest, while the administrative advantage goes to the banks that serve as trustees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a real but uneven advantage: deferring tax on investment earnings helps any saver, but with no contribution ceiling the bulk of the tax benefit would flow to households with large sums to invest, and banks would hold the mandatory trustee role. The cost is deferred federal revenue that other taxpayers ultimately cover. As drafted, it functions more as a wealth-accumulation tax shelter than a broad savings incentive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edgar L. Jenkins introduced the Savers and Investors Act of 1989 on April 3, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill drew two cosponsors, one House Republican and one House Democrat.
No further action was ever taken: the Ways and Means Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a vote in the House before the 101st Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one lost anything tangible, since the bill never advanced; banks and trust companies simply missed a chance at a new trustee business, and wealthy savers missed a new shelter. Ordinary taxpayers were spared an unlimited tax-deferral vehicle whose benefits would concentrate among the affluent.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and ordinary taxpayers; bill died quietly

for.name: Rep. Edgar L. Jenkins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to Ways and Means.

for.name: Two House cosponsors
for.role: 1 of 175 House Republicans and 1 of 257 House Democrats

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got far enough for a partisan split; its tiny sponsorship was bipartisan, with one Democratic sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and one Republican cosponsor.

industries.note: The bill requires every tax-deferred account to be administered by a bank or a trustee the Treasury approves, making banks the mandatory gatekeepers — and fee earners — for any money sheltered under it. It would also impose reporting duties on them.
With no contribution limit, the tax deferral on earnings is worth the most to those with the largest sums to shelter, while the deferred revenue would be made up by other taxpayers.
